It is named Kena. Furthermore,
within this realm of the Heavenly King, the territory is exceedingly vast and the populace is numerous and prosperous.
The king possessed nine hundred elephants, while his other great leaders each had two or three hundred.
Whenever the king personally led his troops into battle,
he constantly fought against the asuras.
The King of Devas is ever victorious.
According to the laws of that kingdom,
he knew himself to have few elephants and few soldiers.
They immediately requested a truce.
Each year they paid taxes,
and no longer engaged in battle or mutual slaughter.
Their clothing, speech,
customs, and social practices are similar to those of the Five Indias.
Only the common people of the villages in Southern India differ in their speech;
they belong to the class of those who serve [others].
The customs of the Central Kingdoms are no different from those of the Five Regions; in their national laws,
there are no stocks, cudgels, or prisons.
Those who commit offenses shall be fined according to the gravity of their crime;
there shall be no corporal punishment or execution, even for the king himself.
Down to the common people,
they did not witness such things as hunting or releasing hawks and dogs;
even if there were highwaymen on the roads who seized property, they would simply release it.
Nor does one kill prematurely;
for if one were to do so according to the nature of sentient beings, there would be harm.
The land is very warm;
the hundred species of plants are perpetually green,
and there is no frost or snow.
Their food consists solely of non-glutinous rice, cakes, parched grain flour, ghee, milk, and curd;
there is no sauce, though salt is used.
They cook their rice entirely in earthen pots before eating it.
There are no iron cauldrons or such items.
The common people have no separate labor taxes;
they merely contribute five *shí* of grain from their fields to the King.
The king himself dispatched people to transport [the grain] for the landowner, yet the latter would not send it.
In that land, the common people were mostly poor and few were wealthy.
In the houses of kings, officials,
and the wealthy, they wear a pair of cotton cloths (*kārpāsa*).
The wealthy have a whole piece;
the poor have half a piece.
It is the same for women.
Whenever that king sat in his hall of audience,
the leaders and the common people would all come and sit surrounding him on all four sides.
Each contended over their respective principles;
lawsuits were manifold and chaotic,
leading to constant disorder and clamor.
The king listened without anger and replied slowly, "This is yours; this is not yours."
Those commoners took the King’s single word as definitive and spoke no further.
The king, his ministers, and other leaders were deeply devoted to and placed great faith in the Triple Gem,
especially in the presence of their preceptors and monks.
The king and the leaders sat upon the ground, refusing to sit upon couches.
The king and the leaders—
Whether walking, sitting, coming,
or going, he would carry his small bed with him and sit down wherever he arrived.
He did not sit upon another’s bed.
In both monasteries and royal residences, three-story towers were constructed; from the bottom, the first story was made into a storehouse.
The upper two stories are inhabited by people;
the various great leaders and others dwell there as well.
All the houses have flat roofs.
Constructed of brick and wood,
those on the outside are all thatched-roof houses resembling those of the desert; they are built to withstand the falling rain and consist of a single story.
The products of the land consist only of cotton cloth, elephants, horses, and various other things;
gold and silver are not produced in that country.
They all come from foreign lands.
Furthermore, they do not raise livestock such as camels, mules, donkeys, or pigs;
their oxen are entirely white.
Among ten thousand heads,
there is rarely even one that is reddish-black;
sheep and horses are extremely scarce.
Only the King maintains two or three hundred people and sixty or seventy horses;
apart from these, neither the leaders nor the common people keep any livestock at all.
They raise cattle solely for the purpose of obtaining milk, curd, and ghee;
the people of the land are virtuous.
There is little killing; in the markets and shops, one does not see places where butchers sell meat.
Here, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are practiced together.
Within this Central Heavenly Realm (Madhyadeśa), there are four great stūpas.
On the northern bank of the Gaṅgā River, there are three great stūpas:

That city has already fallen into ruin;
there is a stupa, but no monks and no common people.
This city is situated at the very edge;

Fourth: Those who go there to pay homage find it exceedingly difficult, and only then do they become enlightened.

Seeing that there were monks at the temple,

The king possessed eight hundred elephants,
and his territory was exceedingly vast,
extending as far south as the Southern Sea.
To the east it reaches the Eastern Sea;
to the west, the Western Sea;

The border regions of West India and East India share similar customs regarding clothing, food, drink, and social manners,

The only difference lies in the slight variation of their speech;
the land is hotter than that of Central India (Madhyadeśa).
As for the products of the land:
There are cotton cloths, elephants, water buffaloes,
and yellow oxen; there are also a few sheep,
but no camels, mules, donkeys, or the like.
There are paddy fields,
but no millet, sorghum, or the like;
as for items such as cotton and silk, they are likewise absent.
Throughout the five regions of India,
there were none [who did not revere them]; the king and the leading citizens alike held the Triple Gem in the highest esteem, and they provided for the temples and the Sangha in abundance.
Both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna practices were carried out there. On that mountain,

These were created by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna and the yakṣa deities;
they were not made by humans.

It is a three-storied tower,
square on all four sides and measuring over three hundred paces in circumference.
During the time of Nāgārjuna, it was as follows:
The monastery had three thousand monks,
yet he alone provided for them with fifteen *shí* of rice;
every day, he supplied the three thousand monks with food.
The rice was never exhausted;
even after being taken, it would grow back again,
never decreasing in its original amount.
However, this monastery is now in ruins and has no monks.
Nāgārjuna lived for seven hundred years.
Only then did he pass away.
At that time, while on the road to South India,

Five-character verse: On a moonlit night, [traversing] the road, Floating clouds drift back with a whistling sound.

My country lies on the northern shore of heaven;
other lands lie at the western corner of the earth.
In the region of Jiamen (Jinam), there are no wild geese;
who then flies toward the forests?
Furthermore, from the southern heavens, one travels northward for two months.
Upon reaching the city where the King of the Western Heaven resides,
this Western Heavenly King likewise possesses five or six hundred elephants.
The local products include cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), silver, elephants, horses, sheep, and oxen.
They produce large quantities of wheat, barley, and various beans,
while rice is very scarce.
Their diet consists mostly of cakes, parched grain flour, curd, and clarified butter.
In their marketplaces, they use silver coins, fine cotton cloth,
and other such goods; the king, the leaders, and the common people alike possess the utmost reverence and faith in the Triple Gem.
The monasteries are numerous and the monks are abundant;
both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are practiced there,
and the territory is very extensive.
To the west, it reaches the Western Sea.
The people of this country are mostly skilled at singing;
the other four heavenly kingdoms are not like this one.

Moreover, this is the law of the Five Indias.
Those who go abroad do not take provisions with them;
wherever they go, they obtain food by means of begging.
Only the king, his ministers, and their leaders set out;

Furthermore, they traveled north from India for more than three months.
He arrived at the northern kingdom,

The king possessed three hundred elephants.
They dwell in cities built against the mountains.
From this point onward to the north,
there are gradually more mountains.
Because their country was narrow and small and they possessed few soldiers and horses,

for this reason, they dwell among the mountains.
The people’s clothing, customs,

however, the climate is slightly colder than that of Central India.
There is neither frost nor snow,

The land produces elephant-hide cloth (*karpāsa*), rice, wheat, and a few donkeys and mules.
That king possessed one hundred horses;
his chief officers had three or five,
while the common people had none at all.
To the west lies a level plain;
to the east, it borders the Snow Mountains.
Within the kingdom, there are numerous monasteries and a sufficient number of monks.
Both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna practices are followed there.
Furthermore, after traveling for one month across the Snow Mountains,
there is a small kingdom to the east.
It is named Subannagotra and is under the jurisdiction of the kingdom of Tibet.
Their clothing is similar to that of Northern India.
The spoken language is distinct [from others],
and the climate is extremely cold.
Furthermore, from this country of Śrīlaṃdā, one travels westward.
After traveling for one month,
he arrived at the country of Śāketa,
where the language and sounds were somewhat different.
They are largely similar in their customs of dress and the products of their land.
The seasonal shifts between cold and warmth are similar to those of Northern India;
it is likewise well-provided with monasteries and monks.
Both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna practices are followed there.
The king, the leaders, and the common people all possess great reverence and faith in the Triple Gem.
Furthermore, traveling west from this country of Cīna for one month, one arrives [at the next destination].
Upon arriving at the kingdom of Puruṣapura (formerly known as Gandhāra),
[one observes] their clothing and customs,
as well as the seasonal variations of cold and heat.
It is similar to Northern India,
though the spoken language differs slightly;
this country has an abundance of camels.
The people of the country take milk and curd to eat.
The king and the common folk alike revere the Triple Gem,
and they provide for the temples and the monastic community in abundance.
He then composed the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.

In this country, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are practiced together.
At present, the Mahāyāna has encroached upon half the kingdom and caused its decline.
From this country, it extends throughout the Five Indias.
I did not drink much wine.

They were excellent abbots,

there was a monastery in the mountains named Nāgārjunīya.

Entering the mountains, he arrived at the kingdom of Kāla;
this Kamira is also among the northern regions of India.
This country is somewhat large;
the king possesses three hundred elephants,
which reside in the mountains.
The roads are perilous and difficult to traverse;
it is not invaded by foreign nations,
and its population is exceedingly vast.
The poor are many and the wealthy are few.
The clothing of the king, the leaders, and the various affluent individuals is no different from that of Central India.
As for the common people outside [the nobility],
they all cover their ugly forms with woolen blankets.
The soil produces copper, iron, cotton cloth, woolen blankets, oxen, and sheep.
There are elephants, few horses, non-glutinous rice, and grapes.
The climate is extremely cold.
It differs from all other countries of former times;
while there is autumn frost and winter snow,
the summer is sufficiently cool and rainy.
The hundred plants are covered in green leaves that are now withering;
the winter grasses are all parched, and the rivers and valleys have narrowed.
It takes five days' journey from north to south.
Traveling east and west for one day,
the land is exhausted;
the remainder is all shaded by mountains.
The houses are constructed with wooden planks and roofs made of wood rather than grass or tiles.
The king, the leaders, and the common people all hold the Triple Gem in profound reverence.
Within the country there was a dragon pond.
That dragon king daily made offerings to an indefinite number of arhat monks.
Although no one saw those holy monks eating, [the offerings were nonetheless made].
After the meal had also concluded,

To this day, offerings have continued without interruption.
When the king and high-ranking chiefs go abroad, they ride elephants;
minor officials ride horses.
The common people all travel on foot.
Within the realm there are sufficient monasteries and sufficient monks;
both Mahayana and Hinayana are practiced together.
According to the laws of the Five Indies,
this applies from the king at the highest level down to the king’s queen and princes.
Down to the leaders and their wives, each according to their own capacity and means,
built monasteries individually;
they did not construct them collectively.
He said, "Each has their own merit;
why must we create it together?"
Since this is so, it is likewise for other princes and others;
whenever one constructs a monastery as an act of offering.
He immediately bestowed villages upon the common people and made offerings to the Triple Gem;
there was no instance where he constructed a monastery in vain without bestowing [land] upon the common people.
This is according to the laws of foreign lands:
the king and his consort each have their own separate villages of subjects.
The princes and their leaders each have their own subjects;
they practice giving freely and do not rule as kings.
The same applies to the construction of monasteries:
when it is necessary to build, one builds,
without even consulting the king.
The king also did not dare to obstruct him,
fearing he would be held accountable for the offense.
This was because he possessed great wealth and many subjects.
Although there was no village from which to receive alms,
he nevertheless exerted himself to build a monastery,
managing it through his own efforts.
They obtain goods to make offerings to the Triple Gem;

It is necessary to bestow upon the common people the villages and gardens.

The land is narrow and small;

The king, the common people,
